Percentage meeting foundational reading / numeracy criteria. Higher is better. Age 7–14 and Grade 2/3 populations remain separate.
Percentage of female 15-year-old students below Level 2. Lower is better. This is not the MICS foundational proficiency percentage.
India NAS, FLS and PRS and Iran PIRLS are retained as distinct measures. Mean scores, correct-answer percentages and proficiency percentages are not interchangeable.
Iran participated in the PIRLS 2021 cycle but assessed one year later. Survey year is retained as 2022.
Original seven-location figures were read from the current selected workbook, which cites the UNICEF 2022 Combined worksheet. They are retained at original precision.
Blank numeric values mean no observation retrieved for that cell. They are not zero and do not establish non-existence.
PIRLS standard error is included. Other extracts lack uncertainty estimates. PISA values are rounded; sampling warnings are retained.
No country or regional pooled averages. Compute survey-weighted proportions from eligible girls, not equal averages of provinces or unrelated measures.
Birth conditions and facilities do not average into learning scores. These extracts cannot estimate causal contributions.
Match birth exposures to the girls’ birth years, school provision to attendance years, and geography to survey boundaries.

Teacher and qualifications shortages: % of students in schools where principals report instruction hindered by missing or inadequately qualified staff. Preschool: % reporting at least one year. All-sex context, not girls-only.
This is an expanded extracted-data release, not a complete microdata download or complete education-indicator panel. Retrieval gaps list outstanding series and source routes.
MICS legacy data retain source precision. New report extracts retain displayed precision. No imputation, interpolation or score conversion.
Source URLs sit beside each dataset. Links in Retrieval gaps are access routes, not evidence of a completed download.
Report evidence and Country alignment supplement the missing data. They do not change missing numeric cells into observed estimates.
Frameworks organise hypotheses. Observational reports identify associations. A randomised trial supports a causal claim only within its intervention, sample and outcome limits.
Match geography, sex, age, assessment, exposure timing and outcome. A same-country report can still be a poor cohort or indicator match.
Qualitative interpretations in Retrieval gaps are proposed analytical pathways, not measured contributions or findings for every selected country.
No confidence percentages, invented coefficients or qualitative-to-numeric scores were assigned. Direction and magnitude need matched empirical testing.
Publication year differs from evidence or survey period. Later reports may interpret older data; current conditions cannot retrospectively explain an earlier cohort.
Use reports to choose variables and pre-specify hypotheses. Estimate separate survey-aware models by comparable outcome; do not average across scales.
2023 is fixed for workforce, GDP and WHO-modelled violence to avoid mixing latest available years. Workforce GDP retains every year 2018–2025; blanks remain missing.
Join national context by ISO3 and year. PAK national context does not replace Sindh observations. GBR childhood supplement covers England and Wales only.

Participation includes employed and unemployed women in the labour force. Employment-to-population measures those employed. Women’s share of the total labour force has a different denominator. All three are retained.
Total GDP measures economic size, not individual prosperity. GDP per capita is also included. Both use current US dollars, not inflation-adjusted or purchasing-power-parity values.

Partner violence concerns ever-partnered women aged 15–49. Non-partner sexual violence concerns women aged 15+. These overlap and must not be summed. These measures do not cover every form of violence.

UNICEF violent discipline is girls aged 1–14 over the past month. Childhood sexual-violence indicators usually use retrospective reports by older women; they do not measure current incidence among young girls.

The World Bank API returned no non-missing observations for the two selected age 15–19 partner-violence series across these countries, 2000–2025. This does not establish that WHO has no adolescent estimates.
DHS, UNICEF, ABS, Statistics Canada, ONS and CDC measures have different acts, perpetrators, age cut-offs and denominators. Compare within the same indicator, not as one ranking.

Discipline years match learning surveys for Nepal, Palestine, Viet Nam, Afghanistan and Thailand 2022, but age ranges differ. Bangladesh 2025 and Mongolia 2023 do not match earlier MICS learning years.
Blank numeric cells mean unavailable or not retrieved, never zero. Violence data records the status and source for every selected harmonised country-indicator combination.

World Bank API provides point estimates without WHO uncertainty intervals. Survey confidence intervals are included only where retrieved. Do not interpret small differences as statistically established.

Use these variables to frame questions about safety, learning opportunities and economic participation. Country-level associations cannot establish individual pathways or the direction of causation. Employment can also reflect economic necessity.
A 2023 context measure cannot retrospectively demonstrate causes of a 2018 education outcome. Select historical economic rows and relevant exposure periods before any explanatory modelling.

Iran has no retrieved values in the selected WHO violence series. Israel lacks retrieved lifetime IPV but has past-year IPV. Girls’ violence coverage is incomplete, including New Zealand. Supplementary national surveys are retained separately.
Sources were retrieved on 10 October 2026. World Bank revisions may change previous values. The source URLs, update dates and exact indicator IDs support reproducibility.
Country-specific change: female population / female population in 2018 × 100. Female population share is separately the percentage of total population.

100 × (value − minimum) / (maximum − minimum), using available observations in the fixed 18-location universe within exact indicator, population, geography level and reference period. Higher means more of the measured quantity, not universally better.
Missing values remain missing. Fewer than two values or zero spread produces no relative index. Reference bounds do not change with dashboard country-group filters.
Female labour percentages and violence prevalence already have specific denominators and are not divided again by female population. GDP per capita retains total-population denominator.
WPS 2025/26 security framework inversion, four equal-weight components. Not prevalence or all forms of violence; inspect the score sheet for components and sources.

Same-year total population across the fixed 27-country set is the denominator. Female contribution = 100 × country female population / combined total population. Country female share = 100 × female / country total. Share of combined females = 100 × female / combined females. Group filtering never changes the denominator.

Estimated count = rate / 100 × matching eligible female population. Contribution = 100 × estimated count / combined total population. Female 15+ is estimated from WDI age shares; labour estimates may use a different population vintage, so counts are approximate. Violence and learning rates are not multiplied by all-age female populations.
Normalised metrics retains the previous min–max calculations for audit only. It is superseded by Population reference and Population contributions for default dashboard comparisons.

Unavailable contributions are blank, not zero. Composite security scores, monetary values, gross ratios and all-sex school-context measures are not treated as female prevalence. Same-year denominator required.

Nine African countries added 13 October 2026; denominator recalculated for 28 countries. Legacy workbook and legacy min–max audit retain original scope. Current complete dashboard data are downloadable as JSON.

UNICEF Combined worksheet, May 2022 edition; children aged 7–14, both sexes. Rural/urban and five wealth-group skill percentages are separate breakdowns. A wealth gap is richest minus poorest, in percentage points. An urban/rural gap is urban minus rural. Retain survey periods and Sindh-only geography.

PISA 2022 OECD country notes, Socio-economic divides. ESCS combines parents’ education, parents’ occupational status and home possessions. Maths gap is top minus bottom within-country ESCS quarter, in score points. Variation is the share associated with ESCS; resilience is the share of disadvantaged pupils reaching the national top maths quarter. These are all-sex enrolled-student measures, not girls-only or causal estimates.

Verified 15 October 2026: 8 MICS locations and 13 PISA locations, 17 distinct locations among the 28. Original survey dates retained. Household wealth/residence and PISA ESCS are different measures, not a combined ranking. Missing locations remain unfilled.

Proportion of women who have ever experienced intimate partner violence (modelled estimate, % of ever partnered women ages 15-49)

Proportion of ever-partnered women ages 15-49 who have ever experienced one or more acts of physical and/or sexual violence by a current or former intimate partner in their lifetime. Physical violence includes acts such as being slapped, pushed, hit, kicked, dragged, choked, burnt, or threatened with or assaulted using a weapon by an intimate partner. Sexual violence refers to being physically forced or coerced into sexual intercourse or other sexual acts, including when unable to consent, by an intimate partner.
The United Nations Inter-Agency Working Group on Violence Against Women Estimation and Data (VAW-IAWGED)  (WHO, UN Women, UNICEF, UNSD, UNFPA, UNODC)
